Community Emergency Drill Arrangements
This document sets out the arrangements for the upcoming community emergency drill,
a simulated exercise designed to test local response coordination. It covers purpose,
participating roles, scheduling, safety protocols, evaluation methods, and record-keeping
duties. The drill is not a real emergency activation; all observations are simulated and
any performance indicators are for internal learning only. No causal claims about actual
incident outcomes are made. The arrangements apply to all volunteers, observers, and
partner agencies involved in the exercise.
A Drill Purpose and Scope
The drill aims to practise evacuation, communication, and resource allocation under
simulated pressure. Scope is limited to the designated community zones and excludes
real emergency dispatch. Participating households receive advance notice, and all
activities remain within the exercise boundary. The exercise does not test real response
times as causal measures; instead, it records simulated observations for after-action
review. The scope also defines which agencies may observe and which may actively
participate.
A.1 Planning and Coordination
A planning committee coordinates logistics, volunteer assignments, and safety briefings.
The committee meets regularly during the preparation period and maintains a shared
checklist. Coordination includes confirming venue permissions, first-aid coverage, and
communication channels. All planning decisions are documented and shared with
participants in advance. The committee also prepares contingency plans for weather or
other disruptions, ensuring the drill remains safe and within the simulated scope.
A.1.1 Roles and Responsibilities
Clear role assignment is essential for a safe and orderly drill. The following subsections
define the duties of controllers, safety officers, and evaluators. Each role has specific
authorities and limits, and all role holders receive a briefing before the exercise begins.
Role holders must not exceed their simulated authority or interfere with real emergency
services. The table below summarises the main duty categories and reporting lines.

A.1.1.1 Controller Duties and Communication
Controllers manage the exercise flow, issue simulated injects, and maintain radio
discipline. They must log every inject and response observation using the provided
forms. Controllers do not direct real emergency resources and must clearly label all
messages as exercise traffic. They report to the chief controller and coordinate with
safety officers before any scenario escalation. Controllers also ensure that participants
understand the difference between simulated and real instructions.
Supporting records are presented in Table 1.
Table 1: Controller duties and reporting lines
A.1.1.2 Safety Officer Authority
Safety officers have absolute authority to pause or stop the drill if they observe a real
hazard. They conduct pre-drill safety checks, monitor participant welfare, and maintain
contact with on-site first aid. Safety officers wear distinctive identification and are
briefed on all simulated hazards. Their stop authority overrides controller instructions.
Any safety intervention is recorded and reviewed after the exercise to improve future
arrangements.

A.1.2 Evaluator Observation Methods
Evaluators use structured observation forms to record simulated actions, communication
clarity, and adherence to procedures. They do not intervene in the exercise except
through safety channels. Observations are timestamped and cross-checked with
controller logs. Evaluators focus on learning points rather than pass or fail judgments.
Their notes feed into the after-action review and help identify training needs. The table
below outlines the observation criteria used by evaluators.

A.2 Participant Briefing and Consent
All participants attend a briefing that explains the exercise objectives, safety rules, and
the voluntary nature of involvement. Consent forms are collected before the drill, and
participants may withdraw at any time without penalty. The briefing clarifies that no real
emergency services will be dispatched and that all communications are simulated.
Participants receive written materials in accessible formats. The table below lists the key

B Schedule and Logistics
The drill schedule is designed to minimise disruption to community routines while
allowing sufficient time for setup and debrief. Logistics cover venue preparation,
equipment distribution, and refreshment arrangements. The schedule includes buffer
periods for safety checks and unexpected delays. All timing is communicated through
multiple channels. The subsections below detail the phased timeline and the resource
allocation plan.
B.1 Phased Drill Timeline
The timeline is divided into preparation, execution, and debrief phases. Preparation
includes site setup and final safety checks. Execution follows a scripted sequence of
simulated events. Debrief occurs immediately after the exercise to capture initial
observations. Each phase has designated leads and checkpoints. The table below
presents the phase schedule with responsible parties and key activities.
B.1.1 Resource Allocation Plan
Resources include volunteers, communication equipment, first-aid supplies, and printed
materials. Allocation is based on zone needs and simulated scenario requirements. A
central cache manages equipment check-in and check-out. Resource shortfalls are
logged for future planning. The plan ensures that no zone is over-resourced at the
expense of another. The subsections below describe equipment staging and volunteer
assignment.
B.1.1.1 Equipment Staging and Checkout
Equipment is staged at the command post and distributed to zone leaders before the
drill starts. Checkout logs record item, quantity, and responsible person. Radios are
tested on designated channels, and spare batteries are available. After the drill, all
equipment is returned and inspected. Damaged or missing items are reported to the
logistics lead. Staging follows a simple layout that keeps walkways clear and access
unobstructed.
B.1.1.2 Volunteer Assignment and Rotation
Volunteers are assigned to zones based on training and availability. Rotation schedules

prevent fatigue during the exercise. Each volunteer receives a role card and knows their
reporting point. Relief volunteers are on standby for unexpected absences. Assignment
adjustments are made through the zone leader and logged at the command post.
Volunteers are reminded that their participation is simulated and that they may raise
safety concerns at any time.
B.1.2 Communication Channels and Protocols
Communication protocols define primary and backup channels for exercise traffic. All
messages begin and end with the phrase exercise, exercise to prevent confusion with
real incidents. Radio discipline is enforced, and sensitive information is not transmitted.

B.2 Post-Drill Review and Reporting
After the drill, the planning committee compiles observations, safety reports, and
participant feedback into an after-action report. The report distinguishes simulated
observations from any real-world claims and avoids causal conclusions. Findings are
shared with participants and partner agencies. Recommendations are tracked for
implementation. The review process emphasises learning, transparency, and continuous
improvement of future drill arrangements.
